key_terms.meaning: A pixel where intensity changes strongly in two different directions, so it stays identifiable when the view shifts slightly.
2×2 matrix of windowed sums of Ix², IxIy, Iy²; its two eigenvalues say how the local patch varies along its two principal directions.
R = det(M) − k·(trace M)² with k ≈ 0.04–0.06; large positive R = corner, large negative = edge, near zero = flat.
A roughly uniform image region that differs from its surroundings; detected as a local extremum of the Laplacian or the Difference of Gaussians over scale.
A stack of copies of the image blurred by Gaussians of increasing σ, so a feature can be found at the size it actually appears.
DoG(x,y,σ) = G(σ₂)∗I − G(σ₁)∗I, a cheap approximation of the scale-normalized Laplacian used to pick SIFT keypoints.
A 128-vector: gradient orientation histograms with 8 bins in each of 4×4 cells around the keypoint, rotated to the keypoint orientation and normalized to unit length.
A faster detector–descriptor: box filters with integral images approximate the Hessian, giving a 64-value descriptor.
Histogram of Oriented Gradients: gradients are binned by direction (usually 9 bins) inside cells (often 8×8 pixels), then contrast-normalized over overlapping blocks.
A cluster centre in descriptor space; every local descriptor is assigned to its nearest centre, which becomes its word index.
The set of k cluster centres produced by k-means on a large sample of descriptors; k is typically a few hundred to a few thousand.
3×3 matrix holding focal lengths fx, fy and principal point (cx, cy): K = [[fx, s, cx], [0, fy, cy], [0, 0, 1]].
Rotation R (3×3) and translation t (3×1) that map a world point into camera coordinates: X_cam = R·X_world + t.
Distance in pixels between a detected image point and the projection of its 3D point using the estimated camera parameters; calibration minimizes its sum of squares.
3×3, rank 2, mapping a pixel x in one view to its epipolar line in the other: x'ᵀ F x = 0.
E = [t]× R, the calibrated version of F; it holds only the relative rotation and translation between two cameras.
In the second image, the projection of the ray from the first camera centre through the matched point; the true match must lie somewhere on this line.
Finding the 3D point where two back-projected rays from matched pixels intersect in the least-squares sense.
Joint nonlinear least-squares refinement of all camera poses and all 3D point positions to minimize total reprojection error.
Assumption that a moving pixel keeps its intensity: I(x, y, t) = I(x + u, y + v, t + 1).
One pixel gives one flow equation with two unknowns (u, v); the motion component along an edge is invisible through a small window.
A least-squares estimate of (u, v) over a small window that assumes the flow is constant inside it.
3×3 invertible matrix with x' ~ H x; it exactly maps one plane seen from two camera positions, or any scene under pure camera rotation.
A similarity measure based on how much knowing the intensity in one image reduces uncertainty about the other; used to register images from different modalities.

takeaways: A corner is defined by change in two directions, so it needs both eigenvalues of a small matrix, not one gradient magnitude.
Harris is rotation-invariant but not scale-invariant; scale space fixes that by searching over blur levels as well as over position.
SIFT and SURF produce descriptors that stay close under rotation, scale change and small viewpoint change, which is what makes matching possible.
HOG ignores which pixel is which inside a cell, so it tolerates small deformation; block normalization makes it robust to lighting.
Bag of visual words converts a variable number of descriptors into one fixed-length histogram, which any classifier can use.
The pinhole model with K, R and t is the single framework behind calibration, stereo, SfM and augmented reality.
Two views of one point are not independent: the match is constrained to an epipolar line, which turns a 2D search into a 1D search.
Stereo depth follows Z = f·B / d, so a small baseline or a small disparity gives a poor depth estimate.
Structure from motion solves for points and poses together; bundle adjustment is what keeps the drift from piling up.
Optical flow gives per-pixel motion but only the component perpendicular to an edge is locally measurable; smoothness priors supply the rest.
bank_note: Long answers here usually want a labelled pipeline (detect → describe → match → estimate) plus the governing equation written out with every symbol defined, and a short note on what the method is invariant to.

bank.q: Define a corner in terms of local intensity change. Show how the Harris detector turns that definition into a 2×2 matrix M and a scalar response R.
outline: A corner changes in two directions; an edge changes in one; a flat region in none.
Shift by (u,v): E(u,v) ≈ [u v] M [u v]ᵀ where M is the windowed sum of Ix², IxIy, Iy².
Eigenvalues λ₁, λ₂ of M: both large = corner, one large = edge, both small = flat.
Avoid the eigen-decomposition: R = det(M) − k(trace M)² with k = 0.04–0.06.
Classify by R: large positive corner, large negative edge, |R| small flat.
Non-maximum suppression and thresholding give the final corner list.

bank.q: Explain scale space and how SIFT uses the Difference of Gaussians to detect keypoints that survive a change of size.
outline: Blur with Gaussian G(σ); stack images over σ to form an octave-pyramid.
DoG approximates the scale-normalized Laplacian; compare neighbouring pixels in space and in scale.
A keypoint is a 3×3×3 local extremum of DoG; sub-pixel and sub-scale fit by a quadratic.
Low-contrast and edge responses are rejected using the ratio of principal curvatures.
Orientation from the gradient histogram of the patch gives rotation invariance.
Descriptor: 4×4 cells × 8 orientation bins = 128 values, normalized.

bank.q: Describe the complete HOG pipeline for a pedestrian-detection style window.
outline: Gamma/colour normalization, then gradient with centred [-1 0 1] masks.
Magnitude and orientation at each pixel; unsigned orientations folded into 0°–180°.
Cells of about 8×8 pixels, 9 orientation bins, soft (interpolated) voting.
Blocks of 2×2 cells, overlapping by half a block; L2-Hys normalization inside each block.
Concatenate all block vectors into one long feature vector.
Classify with a linear SVM; sliding window plus non-maximum suppression at test time.

bank.q: Derive the pinhole camera projection equations from the intrinsic and extrinsic matrices and define every symbol.
outline: World point X, camera point X_c = R X + t, with R 3×3 rotation and t 3×1 translation.
Perspective division: x = f·X_c/Z_c, y = f·Y_c/Z_c.
Homogeneous form: s·[u v 1]ᵀ = K [R | t] [X Y Z 1]ᵀ, s = Z_c.
K = [[fx, s, cx], [0, fy, cy], [0, 0, 1]]; explain focal length in pixels and principal point.
Nonzero s (skew) and the extra radial-distortion terms for real lenses.
3D to 2D loses depth; one view therefore cannot recover Z without extra information.

bank.q: State and explain the epipolar constraint. What does the fundamental matrix encode and what are its degrees of freedom?
outline: x, x' are matched pixels in homogeneous coordinates; x'ᵀ F x = 0.
F = K'⁻ᵀ [t]× R K⁻¹; rank 2, so det F = 0.
F has 9 entries minus one overall scale minus the rank-2 constraint = 7 degrees of freedom.
l' = F x is the epipolar line in the second image; l = Fᵀ x' in the first.
Epipoles are the null vectors: F e = 0, Fᵀ e' = 0.
Estimate F from 8 or more point matches by least squares, then enforce rank 2 by SVD; use RANSAC for outliers.

bank.q: Derive the optical flow constraint equation from the brightness constancy assumption and state the aperture problem.
outline: Brightness constancy: I(x, y, t) = I(x+u, y+v, t+1).
First-order Taylor expansion gives Ix·u + Iy·v + It = 0.
One equation, two unknowns — this is the aperture problem.
Gradient ∇I and time derivative It estimated by filtering consecutive frames.
Motion is only measurable across an edge; along the edge it is invisible.
Additional constraints (Lucas–Kanade window, Horn–Schunck smoothness) complete the system.

bank.q: Define image registration and list the transform models used, from translation up to projective.
outline: Registration = finding the spatial transform T that makes I₂(T(x)) align with I₁(x).
Transform hierarchy: translation (2 parameters), rigid/Euclidean (3), similarity (4), affine (6), projective/homography (8).
Similarity measures: SSD, normalized cross-correlation, mutual information.
Search: feature-based (match keypoints, estimate with RANSAC) or intensity-based (optimize over parameters).
Interpolation is needed when sampling the transformed image.
Assess with target registration error on known landmarks.

bank.q: A Harris matrix M at a pixel is [[100, 20], [20, 25]] and k = 0.04. Compute R, state whether the point is a corner, edge or flat, and explain the sign.
outline: trace(M) = 125, so (trace)² = 15625.
Verify eigenvalues: λ² − 125λ + 2100 = 0 gives λ ≈ 105.6 and 19.4, both positive and sizeable.
Large positive R ⇒ corner.
R ≈ 0 would be flat and R < 0 an edge; the value also sets how large a threshold to use.

bank.q: Explain how to build a bag-of-visual-words image classifier step by step, starting from a set of training images and their class labels.
outline: Detect keypoints (Harris/DoG) and compute a descriptor for each.
Collect a large random sample of descriptors from all training images.
Run k-means with k clusters to obtain the vocabulary of k visual words.
For each image, assign every descriptor to its nearest word and count into a k-bin histogram.
Apply weighting such as TF-IDF and L2-normalize the histogram.
Train a classifier (SVM or nearest neighbour) on the histograms.
At test time repeat detection, assignment and counting, then predict.

bank.q: Describe camera calibration with a planar checkerboard. Cover the homographies, the closed-form estimate of K, and the refinement step.
outline: Print a checkerboard with known square size; photograph it in many orientations.
Detect inner corner points to sub-pixel accuracy; the board plane sets Z = 0.
Each view gives a homography H = K [r₁ r₂ t]; the orthonormality of r₁, r₂ gives two constraints on K.
Three or more views give enough equations for K (Zhang's method).
Recover R and t per view from K⁻¹H.
Refine all parameters by Levenberg–Marquardt on total reprojection error; add radial distortion terms k₁, k₂.
Report RMS reprojection error in pixels; a fraction of a pixel is good.

bank.q: A calibrated stereo pair has focal length f = 800 pixels and baseline B = 0.20 m. Disparity at a point is 40 pixels. Compute the depth and comment on depth error for a disparity error of 1 pixel.
outline: Depth error dZ/Z = −dd/d, so 1 pixel error at d = 40 gives about 0.1 m (10 cm).
At the same depth with a smaller baseline the disparity falls and the relative error grows.
Finer disparity (sub-pixel) or a longer baseline improves depth resolution.
Wrong matches must be removed by left-right consistency and epipolar constraints.

bank.q: Derive the Lucas–Kanade solution for optical flow in a window and state the condition under which it works.
outline: Per pixel: Ix u + Iy v = −It.
Stack over N pixels in the window: A d = b, with d = [u v]ᵀ.
Least squares: d = (AᵀA)⁻¹ Aᵀ b; AᵀA is the structure tensor of the window.
Solvable when both eigenvalues of AᵀA are large — textured patches, not edges.
Iterative warping handles displacements larger than one pixel (image pyramids).
Failures: large motion, occlusion, motion boundaries with a single global flow.

bank.q: Compare SIFT, SURF and HOG as feature representations. Which invariances does each have, and where would you use each?
outline: SIFT: DoG keypoints over scale space; 128-D gradient histogram normalized to keypoint orientation — invariant to scale, rotation and moderate illumination change.
SURF: Hessian with box filters and integral images; 64-D — similar invariance, roughly an order of magnitude faster.
HOG: dense, fixed grid, no keypoint, no rotation or scale invariance; it describes shape over a whole window.
HOG is used for detection (pedestrians, number plates); SIFT/SURF for matching between images, panorama stitching, retrieval.
Evaluating: repeatability of detectors, precision-recall of matches, cost per keypoint.
Plain patch correlation fails on rotation and scale; histogram representations do not.

bank.q: Outline the full structure-from-motion pipeline from an unordered image set, and evaluate where it fails.
outline: Detect and describe features (SIFT), match descriptors between image pairs.
Filter matches with a ratio test; estimate the fundamental or essential matrix by RANSAC; keep inlier tracks.
Choose an initial pair with a wide, well-conditioned baseline; triangulate its points.
Resect new cameras with 3D-2D correspondences (P3P or PnP with RANSAC).
Triangulate new points; repeat with bundle adjustment over growing subsets.
Fix gauge freedom: overall scale, and the 7-dof global similarity.
Failure modes: textureless surfaces, repeated structure, pure rotation (no baseline, no depth), drift, and error from wrong matches.

bank.q: You must align a CT scan to an MRI scan of the same patient. Discuss why intensity-difference measures are unsuitable and how mutual information solves it, and how you would evaluate the result.
outline: CT and MRI grey values have no fixed relationship; the same tissue can be bright in one and dark in the other.
SSD/NCC assume a linear intensity relationship, so they mislead.
Mutual information measures shared information: MI(A,B) = Σ p(a,b) log₂ [p(a,b) / (p(a)p(b))].
Normalized MI reduces sensitivity to overlap size; joint histogram computed over the overlapping region only.
Rigid or affine transform first; optimization by Powell or gradient-based search with multi-resolution.
Evaluate with target registration error on anatomical landmarks, or overlap measures such as Dice if a segmentation is available.

glossary.def: A point whose local intensity pattern changes in two independent directions, making it a repeatable anchor for matching.
The 2×2 windowed matrix of products of image gradients; its eigenvalues measure local variation along two directions.
The scalar R = det(M) − k(trace M)² used to rank candidate corners without computing eigenvalues.
A method that finds roughly uniform regions differing from their surroundings by locating extrema of a Laplacian-like response over both position and scale.
A family of progressively blurred images indexed by σ, allowing features to be detected at their natural size.
A detected image location, often with an associated scale and orientation, that is stable across views.
A fixed-length numeric vector summarizing the neighbourhood of a keypoint so that two keypoints can be compared.
Scale-Invariant Feature Transform: DoG keypoint detection plus a 128-value gradient-histogram descriptor.
Speeded-Up Robust Features: a Hessian-based detector and 64-value descriptor built with integral images for speed.
A precomputed running sum of pixel values so any rectangle sum costs four lookups.
Histogram of Oriented Gradients: local gradient-direction histograms over cells, contrast-normalized over blocks.
A representative descriptor taken as a cluster centre, analogous to a word in a text document.
The codebook of all cluster centres obtained by clustering descriptors; also called the visual dictionary.
Vector of Locally Aggregated Descriptors: for each visual word, store the sum of residuals of its assigned descriptors.
Random Sample Consensus: repeatedly fit a model to a minimal random subset and keep the fit with the most inliers.
An idealized camera in which every scene point projects through the optical centre onto the image plane as x = f·X/Z.
The internal camera numbers — focal lengths in pixels, principal point, skew, distortion — that do not change when the camera moves.
The rotation and translation placing the camera in the world coordinate system.
The pixel where the optical axis meets the image plane, roughly but not exactly the image centre.
Bending of straight lines near the image borders caused by the lens; modelled with coefficients k₁, k₂ in a polynomial of r.
The geometry relating two views of the same scene, captured by the fundamental or essential matrix.
The 3×3 matrix E = [t]× R linking matched points whose cameras are fully calibrated.
Recovering a 3D point from two or more image projections of it, given the camera matrices.
Simultaneous nonlinear least-squares optimization of camera parameters and 3D point coordinates.
The apparent per-pixel velocity field between two consecutive frames of a sequence.
The ambiguity that a small window on a straight edge cannot tell motion along the edge from no motion.
An invertible 3×3 matrix mapping one projective plane onto another; exact for planar scenes and pure rotation.
Estimating the spatial transformation that brings one image into geometric agreement with another.
A similarity measure based on the reduction in uncertainty about one image's intensities given the other's.
